main.description: One language's generation recipe for one kind of headword: the tables its forms are printed in, and the affix rules that fill their cells starting from an entry's lemma. It is a record of its own rather than a field on the language record because rules and tables are large, written per inflection class, and edited at a different cadence than the tag bindings they address. Records prove authorship, not ownership: any user may publish a paradigm for any language and category, and the AppView treats the latest record for a given set of selectors as current, archiving the previous ones. By convention the record key is `{languageID}-{16 hex characters}`, the hexadecimal being a hash of this record's own sorted canonical selector keys — exactly as an eu.leksis.source record's key is computed from its OCLC number. Identity therefore comes from the key: every author's paradigm for one set of categories shares one key by construction, no repository can hold two paradigms for the same set, and `selectors` is immutable for a given identity — changing the categories is publishing a different paradigm, not editing this one. The tables live here rather than on the language record because a real conjugation table is not the cartesian product of a category's axes: it has explanatory headings, cells no combination of features names, and merged cells, so it is authored cell by cell. An entry never stores a generated form: it stores its category and its irregular forms, and a form it asserts itself overrides whatever a rule here would produce for the same cell. That is what lets a language fix a wrong rule once and re-render every entry that uses it, without anybody republishing a record.

languageID.description: Well-formed IETF BCP 47 tag of the language these rules belong to, normalized to lowercase (e.g. "br", "br-gw"). It is repeated here rather than read from the record key alone because the key is a derived string, and a reader holding the record must be able to say which language it describes.

selectors.description: The headword categories these rules apply to — full bundles over what this language declared: a part of speech, the features it calls inherent, and the default value of the category's axis where it names one, e.g. {NOUN, Gender=Masc, Number=Plur} for a Breton anv-kadarn stroll. Each is matched against an entry's own headword bundle by EXACT equality, not by containment: a paradigm selecting {VERB} reaches only entries whose bundle is literally a bare verb, and {VERB, Conjugation=2} is a different paradigm rather than a more specific one. Two paradigms can therefore never both reach one entry. Several selectors are listed here when one set of tables genuinely serves several categories — a declension shared by two genders — which is the only reason this is a list. Immutable for one record key, since the key is derived from it.

label.description: How this language names the paradigm — "first declension", "kentañ displegadur". Optional, and homolingual like every other label in Leksis: the AppView never supplies a name in English for it.

requires.description: Base forms an entry must supply for these rules to run, beyond the lemma. Many languages cannot generate a paradigm from the citation form alone — a Latin noun needs its genitive, a strong Germanic verb its preterite — and this is where a paradigm says so. An entry missing one of these is skipped by this paradigm rather than half-generated, and lands on the language dashboard's missing-forms queue carrying the row's own message.

tables.description: The tables this paradigm is printed in, in the order a reader meets them. Several because one kind of word is often laid out in several grids — the finite forms in one, the participles in another — and because a grid that tried to hold both would need cells for combinations the language does not have.

notes.description: Free-text remarks about the paradigm, in this language: what it covers, which lemmas it is known to mis-generate, where it came from. Prose for other contributors, never rendered to a dictionary reader.

references.description: Where the rules were taken from — a grammar, a treebank, a standardisation body's tables. A paradigm is an assertion about a language and should be able to say who is making it.

subject.description: AT URI of the paradigm record version this record rewrites. An audit trail only: identity comes from the record key, so a rewrite is recognised whether or not this is present, and a `subject` pointing at a record for different categories changes nothing.

createdAt.description: Client-declared creation time of this record version.

table.description: One grid of the paradigm, authored cell by cell. It must tile a rectangle once its cells' spans are accounted for — a row short of a column, or two cells claiming one position, is a table nobody can draw, and the AppView refuses the record for it.

name.description: Caption printed above the grid, in this language — "present indicative". Optional: a paradigm with one table often needs no caption at all.

rows.description: The rows of the grid, top to bottom. A cell spanning several rows appears once, in the row it starts at, exactly as an HTML table writes it — the rows below simply do not repeat it.

row.description: One row of a grid, left to right, skipping the positions cells above already span.

cell.description: One cell of a table. A `title` cell is prose explaining the rows or columns beside it; a `form` cell is an address in the paradigm and the rules that fill it; an `empty` cell is structural filler, the corner where a row heading meets a column heading. Merging is authored rather than inferred: a cell says how many rows and columns it covers, and a form spanning several cells is written as one cell with a multivalue coordinate rather than as several cells that happen to agree.

kind.description: Which of the three kinds of cell this is. Unknown kinds are drawn as empty rather than refused, so a later kind of cell does not break a reader written before it.

text.description: A title cell's text, in this language. Meaningless on the other kinds, which carry no prose of their own: a form cell's heading is the language's label for its coordinates.

coords.description: A form cell's address: which combination of features this cell holds the form of. Required on a form cell and ignored on the others. A coordinate carrying several comma-separated values ("Gender=Fem,Masc") means ONE form covering every cell it names, which is how syncretism is written — the cell is then drawn with a span rather than the form being printed twice. Two form cells of one record must not share an address.

rules.description: How this cell's form is built, in the order the rules are tried: the FIRST row whose condition matches wins the cell — the ordinary Hunspell shape, where one ending takes -ies and another -s. Absent or empty means the cell is manual-only: no rule can fill it, and it is waiting for an entry to write its form out. That is deliberately distinct from a cell whose rules all decline for a given lemma, and a reader is shown the difference.

rowSpan.description: How many rows this cell covers. Absent means one.

colSpan.description: How many columns this cell covers. Absent means one.

requirement.description: "To run these rules, an entry must have supplied this form." It names an address, and the error a contributor sees when the entry has not filled it in.

coords.description: The address of the required form: the cell whose form an entry must have asserted itself. Matched against the entry's own forms exactly first, then by containment, so a form carrying more than the address — an inherent feature repeated on it, or a part of speech a bot wrote in — still answers the requirement.

message.description: What a contributor is told when an entry lacks this form: "the preterite is missing", written in this language. It lives in the rule rather than in the interface because the person who wrote the rule is a speaker, which is what lets the missing-forms queue be homolingual with no translation layer anywhere.

rule.description: One way of building the form of the cell this rule sits in: which form it starts from, the condition that form must satisfy, and the affixes to exchange. A rule with no condition and no affixes is legitimate and means the cell is identical to its base. It carries no address of its own — the cell is the address.

base.description: The form this rule transforms. Absent means the lemma — the entry's canonical orthography — which is the ordinary case. Otherwise it addresses another cell: either one the entry supplies (a `requires` row) or one another cell generates, so a paradigm can build a stem once and inflect it many times. A base that names neither, or a chain of bases that loops, is a defect the AppView refuses the record for.

match.description: A regular expression the END of the base form must satisfy for this rule to apply — Hunspell's affix condition, written as a pattern rather than as a literal so that "any consonant" is expressible. Absent means the rule always applies. It is anchored at the end of the form by the generator, so it must not carry its own trailing anchor. A pattern that does not compile costs the record its place in the index, because a generator that throws would take a reader's page down with it.

strip.description: A literal ending removed from the base before the addition. A base that does not end with it fails the rule, which then does not apply — the same outcome as a condition that does not match.

add.description: A literal ending appended after the strip. Absent means nothing is appended, which is how a rule that only removes an ending is written.

prefix.description: The same exchange at the front of the form, for the augments and mutations a suffix pair cannot express. Applied together with the suffix pair, never instead of it.

affix.description: A literal exchange at the front of a form: what to remove, and what to put in its place. Either half may be absent.

strip.description: A literal beginning removed from the base. A base that does not start with it fails the rule.

add.description: A literal beginning prepended to what remains.

coord.description: One coordinate of a cell address: a bare feature and value, carrying no provenance and no label. Bare because a paradigm is a selection from what the language has already declared, never a second place to declare it — so provenance is read back from the language's own `values` row before the address is displayed or matched against a form.

feature.description: The feature, e.g. "Case". Matched by name, as everywhere else.

value.description: The value, e.g. "Gen". Several comma-separated values mean one form spanning them all ("Fem,Masc").

label.description: How this language names the paradigm, for a reader of this language.

long.description: Full form — the only required half: a lone form is always the full one.

short.description: Optional abbreviated display form; when present it is shown instead of the full form, which appears on hover.

text.description: The reference's display text (a citation, source name or note).

url.description: Optional URL the reference links to.
